blocks.text: Every data project you will ever work on starts the same way: some data sits somewhere, on your laptop, in a shared drive, in a company database, and you need it inside a pandas DataFrame before you can do anything useful with it. That first step, getting data in, is where this lesson lives. It sounds like a small thing. It is not. Getting the read wrong, missing a weird separator, letting pandas guess types badly, loading a file that is too big to fit in memory, causes more real world bugs than almost anything downstream.

blocks.alt: Reading Data CSV, Excel, JSON, SQL
blocks.caption: The most common pipeline in all of pandas: a file becomes a DataFrame in one line.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-615293605.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-615293605.png
1. Introduction

Pandas gives you a dedicated reader function for basically every common data format: read_csv, read_excel, read_json, and read_sql, plus others like read_parquet and read_html that you will meet later in the course. They all follow the same basic shape: point the function at a source, get a DataFrame back. The differences show up in the details, the parameters each one accepts, the assumptions each one makes about your data, and the mistakes each one lets you make if you are not paying attention.

This lesson walks through the four readers you will use the most: CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL. By the end you will know which parameters actually matter day to day, what tends to go wrong with real world messy data, and how to read a genuinely messy file correctly in a single call instead of cleaning it up after the fact.

blocks.title: Why this matters more than it sounds like it should
blocks.content: A huge share of "my model is broken" or "my numbers look wrong" bugs trace back to the very first line of the notebook, the read. A column that silently became text instead of numbers, a date that got read as a string, an index that got duplicated because index_col was left out. Fixing the read is almost always cheaper than debugging everything downstream of it.

blocks.text: 2. Reading CSV Files with read_csv

CSV, short for comma separated values, is the plainest, most common format you will run into. It is just text: rows are lines, columns are separated by commas. No formatting, no formulas, no multiple sheets, nothing fancy. That plainness is exactly why it is everywhere. Almost every tool on earth, from Excel to a random API to a database export, can produce or consume a CSV.
Reading one into pandas is about as simple as it gets.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("sales.csv")
print(df.head())

blocks.text: That single line opens the file, figures out the columns from the first row, guesses a data type for each column by looking at the values, and hands you back a DataFrame. For a clean, well behaved file, this is genuinely all you need. Real files are rarely that well behaved, which is why read_csv ships with dozens of parameters. You will not need most of them. You will need a handful of them constantly.
2.1 The Parameters You Will Actually Use

blocks.alt: The Parameters You Will Actually Use
blocks.caption: Five parameters that cover almost every real world CSV situation.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-333902524.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-333902524.png

sep, sometimes written delimiter, tells pandas what character separates your columns. Not every "comma separated" file actually uses a comma. European exports often use a semicolon because the comma is already taken for decimal numbers. Tab separated files are extremely common too.

code.content:
# Semicolon separated file, common in European exports
df = pd.read_csv("europe_sales.csv", sep=";")

# Tab separated file
df = pd.read_csv("data.tsv", sep="\t")

blocks.text: header tells pandas which row holds your column names. By default pandas assumes row 0, the very first line. Sometimes a file has a couple of junk lines at the top before the real header row, maybe a title or an export timestamp someone left in.

code.content:
# The real column names are on the third line (index 2), not the first
df = pd.read_csv("export.csv", header=2)

# No header row at all, pandas should not treat row 1 as column names
df = pd.read_csv("raw_data.csv", header=None)

blocks.text: index_col tells pandas to use one of the columns as the row index instead of generating a default 0, 1, 2, 3 RangeIndex. This matters a lot when your file already has a natural identifier, a customer id, a timestamp, an order number, that you want to look rows up by later.

code.content:
# Use the order_id column as the row index instead of a plain 0,1,2,...
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv", index_col="order_id")
print(df.loc[10432])   # look a row up directly by its order id

blocks.text: usecols tells pandas to only read specific columns and skip the rest entirely. If your file has forty columns and you only need three of them, this saves real memory and real time, because pandas never even parses the columns you did not ask for.

code.content:
# Only read three of the many columns in the file
df = pd.read_csv("wide_export.csv", usecols=["user_id", "signup_date", "plan"])

blocks.text: dtype lets you tell pandas exactly what type each column should be, instead of letting it guess. Guessing is convenient but not free: pandas has to scan values to decide, and it sometimes guesses wrong, especially for columns that look numeric but should stay as text, like zip codes or account numbers where a leading zero matters.

blocks.title: Why dtype up front beats fixing it after
blocks.content: If pandas guesses a numeric column as text because of one stray non numeric value, every downstream calculation silently breaks or throws an error far from the actual cause. Setting dtype at read time catches that problem on line one instead of twenty cells later.

blocks.text: parse_dates tells pandas which columns hold dates so it converts them into real datetime values instead of leaving them as plain text. Without this, a column full of dates is just a column full of strings that happen to look like dates, and you cannot do date math on strings.

code.content:
# Convert the order_date column into an actual datetime column
df = pd.read_csv("orders.csv", parse_dates=["order_date"])
print(df["order_date"].dt.year)   # only works because it is a real datetime now

blocks.text: 3. Reading Excel Files with read_excel

Excel files show up everywhere in the real world, especially outside pure engineering teams. Finance, sales, and operations tend to live in spreadsheets, and sooner or later that spreadsheet lands in your lap and needs to become a DataFrame.

blocks.title: One setup step CSV does not need
blocks.content: Reading Excel files requires an extra library installed alongside pandas, usually openpyxl. pandas does not bundle it by default because not every project touches Excel. If you get an import error mentioning openpyxl, that is the fix: pip install openpyxl.

code.content:
# pip install openpyxl   (one time setup)
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_excel("quarterly_report.xlsx")
print(df.head())

blocks.text: 3.1 Picking a Sheet with sheet_name

blocks.caption: Real workbooks usually have more than one sheet, and sheet_name is how you pick the one you need.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-263413733.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-263413733.png

An Excel workbook is not always one flat table, it can hold many sheets, one per month, one per region, one per whatever the spreadsheet author decided made sense. By default read_excel reads the first sheet only. Use sheet_name to point at a different one, either by its name or by its position.

code.content:
# By sheet name
df_march = pd.read_excel("quarterly_report.xlsx", sheet_name="March")

# By position, 0 is the first sheet, 1 is the second
df_second_sheet = pd.read_excel("quarterly_report.xlsx", sheet_name=1)

# Read every sheet at once, get back a dict of DataFrames keyed by sheet name
all_sheets = pd.read_excel("quarterly_report.xlsx", sheet_name=None)
print(all_sheets.keys())

blocks.text: That last version, passing sheet_name=None, is genuinely useful when you need to stitch several months or regions together into one combined DataFrame later with pd.concat.
4. Reading JSON with read_json

blocks.caption: JSON is nested by nature, so read_json has to flatten it into rows and columns.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-565580788.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-565580788.png

JSON is the default language of APIs. Web services, mobile apps, and most modern data pipelines pass data around as JSON, so sooner or later you will need to pull it straight into pandas. read_json can take a path to a file or a JSON string directly.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

# From a file on disk
df = pd.read_json("users.json")

# From a JSON string, useful right after an API call
json_text = '[{"id": 1, "name": "Asha"}, {"id": 2, "name": "Ravi"}]'
df = pd.read_json(json_text)

blocks.text: 4.1 The orient Parameter

JSON does not have one single shape. A list of objects, one per row, is the most common layout, but JSON can also be structured as columns mapping to lists of values, or as a nested dictionary of dictionaries. The orient parameter tells pandas how to interpret the structure it is looking at.

blocks.content: {"headers":["orient value","JSON shape it expects","when you will see it"],"rows":[["records","a list of objects, one object per row","the most common shape, especially from APIs"],["columns","a dict of columns, each mapping to a dict of row values","default for read_json, common in exported data dumps"],["split","a dict with separate index, columns, and data keys","used when structure needs to be fully explicit"],["index","a dict of rows keyed by row index","less common, sometimes seen in config style exports"]]}

code.content:
# records orient: a plain list of row objects, very common from APIs
api_json = '[{"id": 1, "score": 91}, {"id": 2, "score": 78}]'
df = pd.read_json(api_json, orient="records")

blocks.title: You do not need to memorize every orient value
blocks.content: In practice you will use records constantly and rarely need the others by name. If read_json gives you back a DataFrame that looks transposed or oddly shaped, that is almost always an orient mismatch, and it is worth checking the raw JSON structure before guessing at fixes.

blocks.text: 5. Reading from a SQL Database with read_sql

blocks.alt: Reading from a SQL Database with read_sql
blocks.caption: read_sql needs two things: a query, and a live connection to run it against.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-52272185.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975212-52272185.png

A lot of real company data does not live in a file at all, it lives in a database. pd.read_sql() lets you run a query and get the results back directly as a DataFrame, no manual cursor handling, no looping over rows to build a table yourself. It takes two things: a SQL query string, and a connection object, usually a SQLAlchemy engine, that knows how to talk to your database.

code.content:
import pandas as pd
from sqlalchemy import create_engine

engine = create_engine("postgresql://user:password@localhost:5432/salesdb")

query = "SELECT customer_id, order_total, order_date FROM orders WHERE order_total > 100"
df = pd.read_sql(query, engine)
print(df.head())

blocks.text: This is convenient in a way that is easy to undervalue until you have done it the manual way once. Without pandas, pulling query results into Python normally means opening a cursor, calling fetchall(), and manually building rows and column names yourself. read_sql collapses all of that into one call and hands you back something you can immediately filter, group, and plot.

blocks.title: Filter in the query, not after
blocks.content: If you only need orders above 100 dollars, put that condition in the SQL WHERE clause, like the example above, rather than pulling every row into pandas and filtering afterward. The database is almost always faster at filtering than pandas is, and you avoid dragging rows across the network that you were only going to throw away.

blocks.text: 6. Comparing CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL

blocks.alt: Comparing CSV, Excel, JSON, and SQL
blocks.caption: Four very different sources, one common destination: a pandas DataFrame.

blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441975213-812828458.png
Each format has a natural home. Knowing which one you are dealing with, and what to expect from it, saves you time before you even open the file.

blocks.content: {"headers":["format","typical use case","read speed","common gotchas"],"rows":[["CSV","flat exported data, logs, quick data sharing between tools","fast, simple text parsing","wrong separator, encoding errors, numbers read as text"],["Excel","business and finance data, multi sheet reports","slower than CSV, extra parsing overhead","needs openpyxl installed, picking the wrong sheet, merged cells breaking structure"],["JSON","API responses, nested or hierarchical data","moderate, depends on nesting depth","wrong orient, deeply nested fields need manual flattening"],["SQL","live production data, large structured datasets behind a database","depends entirely on the query and the database itself","pulling too much data with no WHERE clause, slow or unindexed queries"]]}

blocks.text: 7. Common Real World Gotchas

The functions themselves are simple. The files you point them at rarely are. A handful of problems show up over and over again, across every format, and they are worth knowing before you hit them at 2am debugging a broken pipeline.
7.1 Encoding Errors

blocks.caption: A silent encoding mismatch is one of the single most common first errors beginners hit.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113287-962264947.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113287-962264947.png

pandas assumes UTF-8 encoding by default. Plenty of real files, especially older exports or files created on Windows machines outside the US, are saved in a different encoding like Latin-1 or Windows-1252. Read one of those with the default settings and you get a UnicodeDecodeError, or worse, silently mangled characters in names and addresses that do not throw an error at all.

code.content:
# If the default read fails with UnicodeDecodeError, try a different encoding
df = pd.read_csv("legacy_export.csv", encoding="latin1")

blocks.title: Encoding errors
blocks.content: If read_csv throws a UnicodeDecodeError, do not assume the file is corrupted. Try encoding="latin1" or encoding="cp1252" first, those two cover the vast majority of real world non UTF8 files you will encounter.

blocks.text: 7.2 Thousands Separators in Numbers

Numbers formatted for human readability, like 12,450 or 1,000,000, are extremely common in exported reports, especially from Excel. pandas has no way to know that comma is a thousands separator rather than a literal part of the text, so it reads the whole thing as a string instead of a number.

code.content:
# Without help, "12,450" gets read as the text string "12,450", not the number 12450
df = pd.read_csv("report.csv", thousands=",")
print(df["revenue"].sum())   # now works as an actual numeric sum

blocks.text: 7.3 Memory Blowup from Huge Files

blocks.caption: Reading a massive file in one shot can crash your process before it even finishes loading.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-563767711.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-563767711.png

Calling read_csv on a file loads the whole thing into memory at once. That is fine for a ten megabyte file. It is not fine for a forty gigabyte file, your process will either crawl or crash outright before it finishes reading. Two options exist for this. low_memory=False can help with dtype guessing consistency on large files but does not solve the memory problem itself. The real fix is chunksize, which tells pandas to hand you the file back in pieces, one chunk at a time, so you can process it piece by piece instead of all at once.

blocks.title: More on this soon
blocks.content: This lesson only introduces chunksize as a forward pointer. A later lesson in this course covers chunked and streaming data processing in full, including how to combine partial results across chunks.

blocks.text: 8. Worked Example: Reading a Messy CSV Correctly

blocks.alt: Worked Example: Reading a Messy CSV Correctly
blocks.caption: The goal is always the same: get a clean DataFrame in one call, not a clean DataFrame after five cleanup steps.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-950232337.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-950232337.png
Here is a realistic messy file. It has mixed types in one column, a natural id column that should become the index, and a date column stored as plain text. The raw file looks like this.

Read naively, with no parameters at all, this file causes three separate problems: amount gets read as text because of the commas inside the quoted numbers, order_date stays a plain string instead of a real date, and you end up with a default 0, 1, 2, 3 index instead of using the perfectly good order_id column that is already sitting right there. Here is the same read done properly, in one call.

code.content:
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv(
    "orders_messy.csv",
    index_col="order_id",       # use order_id as the row index
    thousands=",",               # treat commas inside numbers as thousands separators
    parse_dates=["order_date"],  # convert order_date into a real datetime column
    dtype={"customer_name": str},
)

print(df.dtypes)
print(df.loc[1003])

blocks.text: One call, four parameters, and the result is a DataFrame with the right index, real numeric amounts you can sum and average, and real dates you can filter by month or compute time differences on. No follow up cleanup step needed. This is the habit worth building: look at your raw file for a minute before you read it, and set the parameters that match what you see, instead of reading blindly and patching problems after the fact.
9. Choosing the Right Reader

blocks.caption: When in doubt, the source format tells you exactly which reader to reach for.
blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-720074398.png
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785442113289-720074398.png

Every reader in this lesson exists to solve the same problem: get data out of wherever it lives and into a DataFrame. The right choice almost always falls straight out of the source itself. A flat text file with rows and columns is CSV. A file someone built in Excel with multiple tabs is Excel. Data coming back from an API call is JSON. Data living in a company database behind a connection string is SQL. Once the data is in a DataFrame, everything you do next, cleaning, filtering, grouping, joining, works exactly the same regardless of where it came from. That is really the whole point of this first step: it makes the source disappear so you can focus on the data itself.

items: Flat file, plain rows and columns, no multiple sheets: reach for read_csv.
A workbook someone built by hand with several tabs: reach for read_excel and set sheet_name.
Data straight from an API response: reach for read_json and check the orient if the shape looks off.
Data that lives behind a live connection to a company database: reach for read_sql with a SQLAlchemy engine.

blocks.title: One habit to carry forward
blocks.content: Before reaching for any reader, open the raw file or peek at the raw response for a few seconds. Ninety percent of the parameters covered in this lesson exist because someone looked at their file first and noticed the separator, the header row, or the date column needed a little help.
